summary: 1. Start hooks immediately with a specific visual action or direct question, skipping conversational preambles like 'You've used X your whole life.' 2. Focus on visible everyday household phenomena (e.g., baking soda fizz, salt on ice) rather than abstract biological systems or theoretical physics. 3. Keep titles short and clear without textbook subtitles like 'The Biology of Cone Cells Explained.' 4. Keep script length under 36 seconds; longer complex setups (50s+) cause early swipe-aways. 5. Frontload the physical mechanism in sentence one to boost the stayed rate above the channel's 40% threshold.
winning_hooks: Immediate, direct questions about visible reactions (e.g., 'Why does baking soda fizz the moment it hits vinegar?')
Concrete, everyday visual triggers (e.g., 'You've seen trucks dump salt on frozen roads...')
avoid: Wordy conversational setups before reaching the actual question (e.g., 'You've used soap your whole life, but why...')
Abstract or theoretical concepts that lack immediate visual context (e.g., immune system training, lead spheres in a vacuum)
next_experiment: A/B test a 30-second Short on a household science topic: Version A starts instantly with a 7-word direct action question, while Version B starts with a 15-word situational setup sentence.
